Let H be the complete pre-target history, W its retained input window, and I the real-item catalog. Excluding H measures discovery among globally unseen items; excluding only W allows previously consumed items outside the window to compete. These define different tasks even with identical model inputs. For reproducible diagnostics, specify candidate sets explicitly: C_H = (I \ H) ∪ {target} versus C_W = (I \ W) ∪ {target}. With identical scores and tie handling, C_H ⊆ C_W, so the target’s full-history-filtered rank cannot be worse. This follows from set inclusion; it is not evidence of improved modeling.

Repeated targets require an explicit policy. A strict unseen-item task makes targets already in H ineligible: report their count and evaluate eligible cases separately. A target-restored diagnostic retains each target exactly once while excluding other history items; label that exception. Stratify into target unseen in H, repeated within W, and repeated only outside W; report counts and metrics per category and stratum. Research finds aggregate accuracy can conceal substantial repetition/exploration differences. [Li et al., 2023](https://staff.fnwi.uva.nl/m.derijke/wp-content/papercite-data/pdf/li-2023-repetition.pdf)

Compare full-catalog and sampled ranks on identical training-prefix targets, scores, eligibility rules, and ties; exclude padding/mask tokens. For BERT4Rec, withhold the target occurrence, append the reserved mask, and score its final nonpadding position. Earlier occurrences are legitimate history. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690) Record unique-negative sampling, seed, candidate counts, and aggregation. Sampled HR@10 is a distinct quantity and can reverse model comparisons. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) Training-prefix results are in-sample diagnostics; keep the pinned host evaluator unchanged and its validation HR@10 authoritative.
